title: Real estate agent call reluctance: a practical fix for phone prospecting on Mac
metaTitle: Real estate agent call reluctance: free fixes for Mac
description: Real estate agent call reluctance costs you pipeline and income. Here are free fixes for prospecting calls, plus where Lazur helps on Mac.
intro: Real estate agent call reluctance is the habit of putting off or skipping calls you know you should make. Researchers measure it as a trait, and it can affect agents at any career stage. This page covers what it costs, why it happens, and free fixes you can use on a Mac today, with or without Lazur.
tldr: A 2010 Baylor and Keller Center survey of 3,319 agents measured call reluctance with a standard test.
Agents with higher reluctance made fewer contacts the week before, though the article gives no exact counts.
Most causes are about the call itself: fear of judgment, no chance to edit, and interruptions to your day.
The best free fix is a fixed call time written as an if-then plan, which has the strongest support in this research.
Focus and call screening protect the block. Lazur helps with scripts and setup, but it does not make the calls.

blocks.text: Call reluctance rarely looks like a decision. It looks like a busy afternoon. You answer email, tidy the listings folder, and check the market report one more time. The phone stays face down. By the end of the day you have made no calls, and you feel a little guilty. Researchers have a name for this pattern: sales call reluctance.
What real estate agent call reluctance costs you

The first cost is pipeline. A call you skip today is a conversation you do not have next month. In a 2010 Baylor and Keller Center survey, agents with higher reluctance scores had made fewer contacts in the previous week. The article gives no exact counts, so read that as a direction, not a formula. The direction is clear: more reluctance, fewer contacts.

rows: Higher call reluctance went with fewer contacts in the week before (Baylor and Keller Center, 2010).
A fast reply made qualification about 7x more likely (2011 Harvard Business Review study, via Expertise.ai).
Self-employed workers are 54% of this occupation, and the median wage for brokers and sales agents was $52,830 in May 2025 (BLS).

blocks.text: Speed matters most with inbound leads. A 2011 Harvard Business Review study tested web leads at 2,241 U.S. companies. A secondary summary says 37% responded within an hour. It also says a reply within the first hour made qualification about 7x more likely. The original paper is paywalled, and the summary's response split does not add up to a full picture. Use the direction, not the exact split. The study covers inbound web leads, not cold calls. It still shows how a slow phone habit can cost you a lead that was already warm.
Why phone calls feel so hard

The reasons are mostly about the moment of the call, not your sales skill. BBC Science Focus, which cites Alison Papadakis of Johns Hopkins, describes phone avoidance in terms of fear and missing cues. The causes section lists the main ones. Here, focus on what that means for your day. A call is a live event you cannot pause. That is why a plan around the call works better than a pep talk before it.
Experience helps, but it does not end the habit

The Baylor and Keller Center article says less experienced agents showed more call reluctance. It is less common among seasoned professionals, but it can occur at any career stage. If you have been in the business for years and still avoid the phone, you are not failing a test you should have passed already. The habit responds to structure. Experience alone rarely supplies it.
Free fixes you can use without buying anything

None of these fixes needs a paid tool. They work on paper, in a spreadsheet, or in your Mac's settings. Start with the schedule. Then build the list and the script. Protect the block with Focus last, once the block is real. Each fix removes one reason to put off the call. Together they make the call smaller, which is the point.
Set the call time as an if-then plan

The strongest evidence in this set is about plans, not willpower. Gollwitzer and Sheeran's 2006 meta-analysis reviewed 94 independent tests of implementation intentions. These are if-then plans, such as 'If the coffee is finished, then I open my list and dial the first name.' The overall effect on goal attainment was d = .65, a medium-to-large effect. The effect may be inflated by publication bias, so expect a smaller gain in your own week. Write the trigger on a sticky note and keep it near the phone.
Build the call list the night before

Most avoidance starts when you have to decide who to call. Remove that decision from the block. Decide the night before. Open Google Sheets and make five columns: Name, Phone, Last contact, Reason to call, and Next step. Keep one tab for the active list. Sort it by the Last contact column so the oldest names sit at the top. Every row needs a reason to call, or it does not belong on the list. If your brokerage has rules about client data, follow them before you paste names into any tool. The [Google Sheets page for realtors](/for/realtors/google-sheets) covers a deal tracker you can adapt.
Write three lines, then talk

A script removes the blank page. Keep three lines in a note on your Mac. Line one says who you are. Line two gives the reason for the call. Line three asks one question. A usable version sounds like this: 'Hi, this is [your name] with [your brokerage]. I wanted to ask one question about the market in your area. Is now a good time to talk for a moment?' Read it once before the block. Then put the note away. A reader sounds like a reader, so talk in your own words after the first line.
Use Focus to protect the block

A call block fails when a ring or a notification breaks it. Press ⌘ Space, type System Settings, and press Return. Then go to System Settings > Focus and create a Focus for prospecting. Under Allowed People, choose Contacts or Favorites, so your clients and team can still reach you. Turn on repeated calls, which lets a call through when someone calls twice within three minutes. Schedule the Focus by time, so it starts when your block starts.
Screen unknown callers without losing leads

The Phone app on Mac can screen unknown callers. Choose Phone > Settings > Calls. Call Filtering can send unknown callers to voicemail. Screen Unknown Callers can ask the reason for the call, and the Phone app rings only after the caller gives a name and reason. This keeps spam away from your block. It can also keep out a new buyer who does not want to explain. Decide that trade-off before you turn it on. Apple's help page lists macOS 27 and macOS Tahoe 26 without saying which steps apply to which version. It also does not say whether calls on your Mac need an iPhone. Check your own setup.
Tools that already do calling

If you want calling built into a customer system, compare the options on their own pages. Follow Up Boss lists its Grow plan at $69 per user per month, with calling as a $39 per user add-on. Its pricing page lists a mobile app and a web app for calling, and it does not mention a native Mac app. Check the pricing page before you decide, because plans change. You do not need a CRM to start a call block.
A worked example of one week

Here is how a first week can run in plain terms. On the first day, you build the list and stop there. On the second day, you set Focus and screen your calls. On the third day, you write the three lines. The first real block comes on the fourth day, and you call only the names on the sheet. On the fifth day, you check what you did, not what you planned.

Take one row from a past open house. The note says the person asked about a quiet street. The reason to call is that question, so your opening can mention it. The next step is a date in the Next step column. The row removes the guesswork, which is where many agents stall. Repeat the same week next time with a longer list.
Follow-up is where the habit keeps going

It is easy to treat the call as the whole job. Send a short email while the conversation is fresh. In Gmail, go to Settings > See all settings > Advanced, then turn on Templates. Save two or three short follow-ups, so you are not writing from scratch after every call. Hold fn to dictate a call note at the cursor, then paste it into your sheet. Read every draft before you send it. [Gmail for realtors on Mac](/for/realtors/gmail) covers templates and scheduled sends in more detail.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥⌘ and ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a control is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. Lazur does not click buttons or operate other apps for you. It guides and drafts. You make the change, and you make the call.
Mistakes that keep the habit alive

items: Researching before every call. Reading one more market report feels productive, but it replaces the call.
Making the block too long. A long block gives you a reason to start tomorrow, so keep it short and repeat it.
Calling only people you like. Warm calls are a fine start, but the list should include a few names that make you uneasy.
Reading the script aloud as a speech. Three lines is the point. Stop after the question and listen.
Skipping the record. If you do not log contacts, you cannot tell whether the plan works, and you will drift back.

blocks.text: Privacy and client data

Your contact list is client data. Before you paste names, phone numbers, or call notes into any AI tool, check your brokerage's rules. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. The product says audio and screenshots go to AI providers to answer and are not stored. It also says content is never used to train AI models. Those are the company's statements. Read the current privacy terms before you rely on them.

faq.question: Is real estate agent call reluctance the same as being bad at sales?
faq.answer: No. Researchers treat call reluctance as its own measured trait. It is less common among seasoned agents, but it can show up at any career stage. A set time and a short list give the habit something to attach to.

faq.question: Do I have to cold call strangers to get clients?
faq.answer: The sources here do not compare cold calls with other methods, so that question stays open. Run a short test on your own list. Track which names lead to real conversations, and keep doing more of what works.

faq.question: Can Lazur make the calls for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, operate other apps, or place calls for you. It can point at things, guide you one click at a time, answer out loud, draft text, and dictate notes at the cursor. You make the call.

faq.question: Does Lazur listen to my calls?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. According to the product, audio and screenshots go to AI providers to answer and are not stored. Check the current privacy terms and your brokerage's rules before you use it near client conversations.

faq.question: Is there a free trial?
faq.answer: Yes. Lazur has a three-day Pro trial with no credit card. It starts when you first open the app. After that, Pro is $18 a month, or $15 a month billed annually, with 150 AI actions. Dictation is unlimited on both plans.

faq.question: Does Apple's Phone screening on Mac need an iPhone?
faq.answer: Apple's help page for the Phone app on Mac does not say. It lists macOS 27 and macOS Tahoe 26 without naming which steps apply to each. Test the setting on your own Mac before you rely on it for client calls.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on macOS, on both Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available.

faq.question: Is it safe to paste my client list into an AI tool?
faq.answer: Check your brokerage's rules first. Client names and phone numbers are personal data, and your brokerage may set its own limits. If the rules allow it, keep the list small and remove notes you do not need.

faq.question: How long before the habit gets easier?
faq.answer: The sources here do not give a timeline, so do not promise yourself a date. Track your contacts each week. If the count rises, the plan is working even if the calls still feel hard.

faq.question: What if a real client calls during my Focus block?
faq.answer: Repeated calls let a call through when someone calls twice within three minutes. Allowed People can also let through contacts and Favorites. Add frequent clients to Favorites so they reach you during the block.

costs.title: Pipeline you never see
costs.text: A missed call does not show up as a loss. It shows up as a conversation that never happened. Baylor and Keller Center found that higher call reluctance went with fewer contacts in the week before. You will not see that gap on a report, so track contacts on purpose.

costs.title: Slow replies to new leads
costs.text: Speed matters with inbound leads. A 2011 Harvard Business Review study found that a fast reply made qualification about 7x more likely. Cold calls work differently, but the same habit slows you down when a lead does reach you.

costs.title: Income in a one-person business
costs.text: Most real estate sales agents work for themselves. BLS reports that 54% of this occupation is self-employed. The median annual wage for brokers and sales agents was $52,830 in May 2025. When you skip the phone, nobody else covers the gap.

costs.title: Time lost in your head
costs.text: Avoidance also costs time you do not log. You plan the call, dodge it, and then feel guilty about the dodge. The sources here do not measure that cost, so treat this as a judgment, not a number.

causes.title: Fear of judgment
causes.text: You may expect a sharp answer, a hang-up, or a stranger who thinks you are a pest. BBC Science Focus names fear of judgment as a main driver of phone avoidance. The call feels like a test you can fail in real time, with no chance to step back.

causes.title: Missing face and body cues
causes.text: On a phone you cannot see a face, a shrug, or a glance at the clock. You guess what the other person means, and guessing feels risky. BBC Science Focus lists this loss of cues as one reason people avoid calls.

causes.title: No chance to edit
causes.text: Email lets you reread and fix a sentence before it leaves. A live call does not. The words come out at once, and that permanence makes some people wait for a better moment that never arrives.

causes.title: Interruptions to your day
causes.text: A ring breaks your focus, so the call feels expensive before it starts. BBC Science Focus notes that calls interrupt the day, which makes them easy to postpone. The fix is a protected block, not a surge of willpower.

causes.title: Less experience
causes.text: The Baylor and Keller Center survey found that less experienced agents showed more call reluctance. The habit is less common among seasoned professionals, but it can occur at any career stage. Experience helps, though it does not remove the need for a plan.

causes.title: No fixed time
causes.text: Without a set time, the call has no start. You wait for a good moment, and the good moment rarely arrives. Research on implementation intentions suggests a written if-then trigger helps people follow through on goals.

fixes.title: Set a call time as an if-then plan
fixes.text: Pick one daily time and write an if-then trigger. The 2006 meta-analysis by Gollwitzer and Sheeran found that plans like this improve goal attainment, with an overall effect of d = .65 across 94 tests. The effect may be inflated by publication bias, so use the plan as a start, not a guarantee.

fixes.title: Build the list the night before
fixes.text: Decide who to call while you are calm, not in the middle of the block. Keep five columns in a Google Sheets tab: Name, Phone, Last contact, Reason to call, and Next step. A row without a reason does not go on the list.

fixes.title: Write three lines, then talk
fixes.text: Keep one opening, one reason, and one question on a note. Read them once before the block. After the first line, talk like yourself. A script is a starting point, not a speech you must finish.

fixes.title: Protect the block with Focus
fixes.text: Go to System Settings > Focus, allow contacts and Favorites, turn on repeated calls, and schedule the Focus to start with your block. A caller who rings twice within three minutes still gets through. Test it once before the first real block.

fixes.title: Screen unknown callers, knowing the cost
fixes.text: Phone > Settings > Calls can screen unknown callers and ask why they are calling. This keeps spam out of your block. It can also stop a new lead who will not explain. Decide that trade-off on purpose, and check the setting on your own Mac.

fixes.title: Follow up in Gmail while the call is fresh
fixes.text: Save a few short follow-up templates in Gmail under Settings > See all settings > Advanced. Send within the hour after the call, while the details are still fresh. Hold fn to dictate notes at the cursor, then read every draft before you send it.

fixes.title: Track contacts, not intentions
fixes.text: Count the people you actually reached each week. The Baylor and Keller Center survey linked higher reluctance with fewer contacts, so the count is the signal to watch. A plan you do not measure tends to drift.

fixes.title: Start with people who already know you
fixes.text: A warm call is usually an easier first call. Start with past clients and people you already know, then add colder names one at a time. The sources here do not compare the two groups, so track which one gives you conversations.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Build the list
plan.text: Open Google Sheets and make five columns: Name, Phone, Last contact, Reason to call, and Next step. Add the names you already know. Every row needs a reason to call before it stays on the list.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Set the Focus
plan.text: Open System Settings > Focus and set up a prospecting Focus. Allow contacts and Favorites, turn on repeated calls, and schedule it to start with your block. Ask Lazur to walk you through any screen you cannot find.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Write the three lines
plan.text: Write three lines in a note: who you are, why you are calling, and one question. Read them aloud once. Put the note away, then say the opening from memory.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Run the first block
plan.text: Start the block at the set time. Work the list from the top. Do not research a name before the call unless the sheet gives you a reason to.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Review what you reached
plan.text: Count the people you reached, not the calls you planned. Write one next date for each name. Move the rest to next week's tab.
